findings.issue_text: app/models/optimized_image.rb:149 — The new downsize definition replaces the earlier Ruby method, causing existing five-argument calls to raise ArgumentError and four-argument calls to interpret height as opts, breaking image processing.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/lib/utilities.js:182 — The unconditional 10 MB limit overrides the configured attachment limit, rejecting permitted attachments when the setting exceeds 10 MB and allowing oversized attachments through client validation when the setting is lower. Apply the new limit only to images.

goldens.comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same core issue: the hardcoded 10 MB (10 * 1024 KB) limit ignores the configurable site settings for different file types. The golden comment mentions that maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], while the candidate issue describes the same problem - that the unconditional 10 MB limit overrides configured attachment limits, causing mismatches between client-side and server-side validation. Both point to the same bug where the hardcoded value doesn't respect per-type settings.
